overview:
Nahash the Ammonite besieges Jabesh-gilead and names his price for a treaty: every man of the town loses his right eye. The town’s messengers reach Gibeah just as Saul comes in from the field behind his oxen. The Spirit of God comes on him; he cuts a yoke of oxen in pieces, sends them through Israel with a threat, and the army that gathers at Bezek crosses over and breaks the Ammonites by midday. When the people demand the deaths of the men who had scorned him, Saul refuses, and Samuel leads everyone to Gilgal to “renew the kingdom.”

Saul becomes king in stages. Samuel anointed him in private (10:1), the lot chose him in public (10:20–24), and some still asked, “How shall this man save us?” (10:27). Only here, after a victory, does all Israel make him king “before the LORD in Gilgal” (v. 15).

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. The Talmud credits Samuel, with Gad and Nathan completing it (1 Chronicles 29:29); many scholars see it as part of a larger history compiled in the 7th–6th century BC from older sources.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it soon after the events (11th–10th century BC); many scholars date its final form to the 7th–6th century BC, drawing on older court and prophetic sources.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: The start of Saul’s reign. Acts 13:21 gives him forty years; conventional dates put his reign about 1050–1010 BC.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Jabesh-gilead east of the Jordan; Gibeah of Saul in Benjamin; Bezek, where the army musters west of the Jordan; and Gilgal near Jericho.

hermeneutics:
The Masoretic text opens the chapter abruptly, but the oldest surviving Hebrew copy of Samuel, 4QSam-a from Qumran (1st century BC), has an extra paragraph just before it. There Nahash, king of Ammon, has been oppressing the tribes of Gad and Reuben east of the Jordan, gouging out each man’s right eye; seven thousand men escape him to Jabesh-gilead, and about a month later he besieges the town. The NRSV prints the paragraph at the end of 10:27. Frank Moore Cross and others hold that a copyist’s eye skipped it; others read it as a later expansion. Either way it changes v. 2. Nahash is not inventing a cruelty on the spot. He has followed refugees to their shelter, and his terms are a policy his victims already know.

Jabesh-gilead lay in the hills east of the Jordan valley. Most scholars place it at Tell el-Maqlub on the Wadi Yabis, a stream that seems to keep the town’s name, and Eusebius put it six miles from Pella on the road to Gerasa. Saul musters at Bezek, west of the river, so the promise “to morrow, by that time the sun be hot” (v. 9) means a night march down into the valley, across the Jordan, and up the other side. Israel divided the night into three watches (Judges 7:19 names “the middle watch”), and Saul’s three companies strike in “the morning watch” (v. 11), the last of them, before dawn. The same town’s men would later walk all night in the other direction to recover Saul’s body (31:11–13).

breakdown.label: Nahash besieges Jabesh and demands their right eyes
Gibeah weeps; Saul comes in from the field
The Spirit, the oxen in pieces, and the muster at Bezek
Word to Jabesh; Ammon routed in the morning watch
Saul spares the men who scorned him
The kingdom renewed at Gilgal with peace offerings

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence, from a threat to a coronation.

rows.text: The threat and the seven days

notes: **Saving:** the elders ask for anyone who will “save” them (v. 3, *moshia*); the messengers promise “help” (v. 9) and Saul announces that the LORD has wrought “salvation” (v. 13), both the noun *teshuah*. The question of 10:27, “How shall this man save us?”, gets its answer, and Saul gives the credit away.

**Two names together:** Saul summons Israel to come out “after Saul and after Samuel” (v. 7), and the chapter ends with both at Gilgal (vv. 14–15). The new king still moves under the prophet’s authority.
**Time pressure:** seven days’ respite (v. 3), “to morrow” twice (vv. 9, 10), and “this day… to day” (v. 13) keep the clock running until the rescue.

Chapters 11–12 close the story of how Saul became king. Chapter 11 settles the doubt of 10:27 and brings the people to Gilgal (vv. 14–15), where Samuel gives his farewell speech in chapter 12. Saul’s wars, and his rejection, begin in chapter 13.

**Backward and forward:** the Church’s footnote at v. 7 points to Judges 19:29, where a Levite sends the pieces of his concubine through Israel. Jabesh had refused that earlier muster and was destroyed, its surviving daughters given to Benjamin (Judges 21:8–12). Now a Benjamite king rescues it, and its men repay him at his death (31:11–13).

traditions.text: The Greek translation tells the story a little differently. It counts the muster at Bezek as 600,000 men of Israel and 70,000 of Judah, double the Hebrew’s Israel and more than double its Judah, and it has the men of Jabesh give their deceptive answer of v. 10 directly to Nahash. At Gilgal it says Samuel “anointed Saul there to be king,” where the Hebrew has the people make him king, and it ends with Samuel and all Israel rejoicing where the Hebrew names Saul. Josephus agrees on the anointing: Samuel poured the holy oil on Saul a second time in front of the crowd, and from then on, he says, Israel’s government was a kingdom.

Josephus knows the background found in 4QSam-a. Before Jabesh, he says, Nahash had already overrun the Israelites beyond the Jordan and put out the right eye of everyone who surrendered or was captured. His reason was military: a soldier fights with his shield in his left hand, so a man without his right eye would be blind “when their left eyes were covered by their shields.” Only then does Nahash march on Jabesh, which Josephus calls the chief city of Gilead.

His Saul promises the messengers help on the third day and a victory before sunrise, so that the rising sun would find Jabesh already free. He cuts the sinews of his oxen rather than cutting them in pieces, and his numbers are larger still: 700,000 besides 70,000 of Judah. Saul marches all night, attacks before sunrise, kills Nahash himself, and then lays Ammon waste. When the crowd demands the doubters’ deaths, Saul swears that no one of “the same lineage with themselves” will die on a day God has given them, and turns the people to feasting.

Rashi tells his readers to take Nahash’s demand literally. He then reports a midrash that reads it as a figure: the “right eye” is the Torah, given from God’s right hand, and Nahash wanted it burned because it says an Ammonite may not enter the congregation of the LORD (Deuteronomy 23:3). In this reading the siege is an attack on the law that kept Ammon out, and the “reproach upon all Israel” of v. 2 is the burning of its Torah. Radak reports the same midrash in his own commentary, so it was well known to medieval readers.

On v. 14 Rashi explains why the kingdom had to be “renewed” at all. At the first choosing there had been opposition (10:27); now, after Jabesh, everyone agreed. He reads v. 12, “Shall Saul reign over us?”, as the mocking question of those earlier doubters, which the people now want punished. Saul’s refusal leaves the doubters alive and lets the whole people, scoffers included, confirm the king together.

The Aramaic translation makes the doubters’ words in v. 12 a flat judgment: they had said Saul was not fit to reign over them. In v. 7 it has dread “from before the Lord” fall on the people, its usual way of keeping God at a reverent distance, and they go out “as one man.”

Kimhi asks why Saul’s summons names Samuel at all. Not everyone had yet accepted Saul as king, he answers, so a man unwilling to follow Saul would still turn out for Samuel, and the muster would be quick. He also explains the setting of v. 14: Samuel chose Gilgal to honor the place where the ark and the tent of meeting first stood when Israel entered the land, even though the tabernacle had since moved to Nob. The renewal, in his reading, was a second acclamation won by the victory over Nahash.

In his questions on the books of Kingdoms, the Syrian bishop gives the same explanation as Josephus. A man who holds his shield toward the enemy with his left hand hides his left eye and sights the enemy with his right, so “he therefore that plucks out that eye, makes men useless in war.” John Hudson quoted the note in his edition of Josephus, and Whiston carried it into his English translation of 1737, so the Jewish historian and the Christian bishop reached English readers side by side.
